theory.overview: Big O Notation is the mathematical language we use to describe the efficiency of algorithms. It tells us how much an algorithm's resource requirements (time or space) grow relative to the input size. Think of it as a way to compare algorithms fairly—by focusing on their growth patterns rather than machine-specific details. When we say an algorithm is $O(n)$, we're saying its running time grows linearly with the input. If we double the input, we roughly double the time. This notation ignores constants and lower-order terms because as $n$ becomes very large (millions or billions), those smaller factors become irrelevant. Big O gives us the upper bound—the worst-case scenario—ensuring our algorithm will never perform worse than this bound.

sections.title: Why Big O Matters
sections.content: Imagine you're choosing between two routes to work. Route A takes 20 minutes regardless of traffic. Route B takes 5 minutes with no traffic, but 2 hours during rush hour. Big O helps us analyze the worst-case scenario so we can make informed decisions. In computing, we care about scalability—how algorithms behave when inputs grow from hundreds to millions of items. An $O(n^2)$ algorithm might be fine for 100 items (10,000 operations), but becomes unusable at 1 million items (1 trillion operations). Understanding Big O helps you write code that won't break when your user base grows.
keyPoints: Big O describes growth rate, not exact runtime
It enables fair comparison between algorithms
Helps predict performance at scale
Focuses on worst-case scenarios

sections.title: The Mathematics Behind Big O
sections.content: Formally, $f(n) = O(g(n))$ means there exist positive constants $c$ and $n_0$ such that $0 \leq f(n) \leq c \cdot g(n)$ for all $n \geq n_0$. In plain English: after some point ($n_0$), $f(n)$ is always bounded above by a constant multiple of $g(n)$. This is why we drop constants: $O(2n) = O(n)$ because we can choose $c=2$. We also drop lower-order terms: $O(n^2 + n) = O(n^2)$ because as $n \to \infty$, the $n^2$ term dominates. The notation focuses on the asymptotic behavior—what happens as $n$ approaches infinity.
keyPoints: f(n) ∈ O(g(n)) iff ∃ c, n₀ > 0: ∀ n ≥ n₀, f(n) ≤ c · g(n)
Drop constants: O(2n) = O(n)
Drop lower-order terms: O(n² + n) = O(n²)
Focus on asymptotic behavior as n → ∞

sections.title: Common Complexity Classes
sections.content: Different problems require different amounts of resources. Here are the most common complexity classes you'll encounter, ordered from fastest to slowest growth:
keyPoints: O(1): Constant time - Array access, hash lookup
O(log n): Logarithmic - Binary search, balanced BST
O(n): Linear - Single loop, finding max
O(n log n): Linearithmic - Efficient sorting
O(n²): Quadratic - Nested loops, bubble sort
O(2ⁿ): Exponential - Subset generation
O(n!): Factorial - Permutations, TSP brute force

sections.title: Analyzing Code for Big O
sections.content: To determine Big O, count the fundamental operations relative to input size $n$. A single loop from 1 to $n$ is $O(n)$. Nested loops where both iterate $n$ times are $O(n^2)$. However, if loops are sequential (not nested), we add their complexities: $O(n) + O(n) = O(n)$. For recursive functions, write a recurrence relation. For example, merge sort: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$, which solves to $O(n \log n)$ by the Master Theorem.
keyPoints: Count fundamental operations relative to input size n
Single loop: O(n)
Nested loops: O(n²)
Sequential loops: O(n) + O(n) = O(n)
Recursive functions: write recurrence relation

examples.analysis: Nested loops, each n iterations: $n \times n = O(n^2)$

sections.title: Space Complexity
sections.content: Space complexity measures additional memory needed as input grows. $O(1)$ space means constant extra memory (a few variables). $O(n)$ space means memory grows linearly with input (e.g., creating a copy of the array). Recursive algorithms use stack space—each recursive call adds a frame. A recursive function with depth $n$ uses $O(n)$ stack space, even if it uses $O(1)$ heap space.
keyPoints: Space complexity ignores input size itself
Counts only additional/auxiliary space
Recursive calls consume stack space
Trade-offs exist between time and space

sections.title: Best, Average, and Worst Case
sections.content: Big O typically describes worst-case, but understanding all three scenarios is crucial. Best case: minimum time for any input of size $n$. Average case: expected time over all possible inputs. Worst case: maximum time for any input of size $n$. For Quick Sort: best and average are $O(n \log n)$, but worst case (already sorted input with bad pivot) is $O(n^2)$. We usually care about worst case for guarantees, but average case for realistic expectations.

keyConcepts.name: Asymptotic Analysis
keyConcepts.description: Studying algorithm behavior as input size approaches infinity. We care about the limiting behavior, not small inputs.

keyConcepts.name: Tight Bounds
keyConcepts.description: $O$ gives upper bound, $\Omega$ gives lower bound, $\Theta$ gives tight bound (both upper and lower).

keyConcepts.name: Amortized Analysis
keyConcepts.description: Average time per operation over a sequence. Some operations are expensive but rare, keeping the average low.
keyConcepts.example: Dynamic array doubling: individual insert is $O(n)$ but amortized is $O(1)$

keyConcepts.name: Master Theorem
keyConcepts.description: Solves recurrences of form $T(n) = aT(n/b) + f(n)$ for divide-and-conquer algorithms.

complexity.timeComplexity: Analyzing algorithms: $O(n)$ to $O(n^2)$ depending on code structure
complexity.spaceComplexity: $O(1)$ auxiliary for analysis, varies by algorithm

steps.title: Identify the Input
steps.description: Determine what $n$ represents. Is it array length? Number of nodes? Input bits?

steps.title: Count Operations
steps.description: Identify fundamental operations (comparisons, assignments, arithmetic) inside loops.

steps.title: Analyze Loop Structure
steps.description: Single loop = $O(n)$, nested loops multiply, sequential loops add.

steps.title: Express Final Big O
steps.description: State the tightest upper bound that describes the growth rate.

practiceProblems.title: Single Loop Analysis
practiceProblems.description:
What is the time complexity of this code?
```python
for i in range(n):
    print(i)
```
practiceProblems.explanation: The loop runs exactly $n$ times, performing one operation per iteration. Time grows linearly with input.
hints: Count how many times the loop executes

practiceProblems.title: Nested Loops
practiceProblems.explanation: Outer loop runs $n$ times. For each outer iteration, inner loop runs $n$ times. Total: $n \times n = n^2$ operations.
hints: The inner loop runs completely for each outer iteration

practiceProblems.title: Sequential Loops
practiceProblems.description:
What is the complexity?
```python
for i in range(n):
    print(i)
for j in range(n):
    print(j * 2)
```
practiceProblems.explanation: Sequential (non-nested) loops add: $O(n) + O(n) = O(2n) = O(n)$. We drop the constant 2.
hints: Loops are not nested inside each other
Drop constant factors in Big O

practiceProblems.title: Logarithmic Loop
practiceProblems.description:
Analyze:
```python
i = n
while i > 1:
    i = i // 2
```
practiceProblems.explanation: $i$ is halved each iteration. Starting at $n$, it takes $\log_2 n$ steps to reach 1. This is the hallmark of logarithmic complexity.
hints: Track how $i$ changes: $n, n/2, n/4, n/8, ...$
How many times can you halve $n$ before reaching 1?

practiceProblems.title: Triangle Pattern
practiceProblems.explanation: Inner loop runs $i$ times where $i$ goes from 0 to $n-1$. Total operations: $\sum_{i=0}^{n-1} i = \frac{n(n-1)}{2} = O(n^2)$.

practiceProblems.title: Three Nested Loops
practiceProblems.explanation: Each loop runs $n$ times independently. Total: $n \times n \times n = n^3$.
hints: Multiply the bounds of all nested loops

practiceProblems.title: Mixed Loop Pattern
practiceProblems.explanation: First part is $O(n^2)$, second is $O(n)$. We keep the dominant term: $O(n^2) + O(n) = O(n^2)$.

practiceProblems.title: Array Access
practiceProblems.description: What is the time complexity of accessing `arr[i]` in an array?
practiceProblems.explanation: Arrays store elements contiguously in memory. The address of `arr[i]` is computed as `base_address + i × element_size`. This arithmetic takes constant time regardless of array size or index.
hints: Address calculation is arithmetic: base + offset

practiceProblems.title: Binary Search Analysis
practiceProblems.description: A binary search algorithm repeatedly divides a sorted array in half. What is its time complexity?
practiceProblems.explanation: Each comparison eliminates half of the remaining elements. Starting with $n$ elements, after $k$ steps we have $n/2^k$ elements. We stop when $n/2^k = 1$, meaning $k = \log_2 n$.
hints: Each step halves the search space
How many times can you divide $n$ by 2?

practiceProblems.title: Recursive Fibonacci
practiceProblems.explanation: The recurrence is $T(n) = T(n-1) + T(n-2) + O(1)$. This forms a binary tree of calls with height $n$, giving roughly $2^n$ nodes. The exact bound is related to the golden ratio.
hints: Tree height is $n$, so roughly $2^n$ nodes

practiceProblems.title: Merge Sort Analysis
practiceProblems.description: Merge sort divides the array in half, sorts each half recursively, then merges. What is its time complexity?
practiceProblems.explanation: Recurrence: $T(n) = 2T(n/2) + O(n)$. The merge step takes $O(n)$. By the Master Theorem or recursion tree: $\log n$ levels, each doing $O(n)$ work, totaling $O(n \log n)$.

practiceProblems.title: Space Complexity of Recursion
practiceProblems.description: What is the space complexity of a recursive function that makes $n$ nested recursive calls before returning?
practiceProblems.explanation: Each recursive call adds a stack frame. If the recursion depth is $n$, we need $O(n)$ stack space even if we only use $O(1)$ variables in each call.
hints: Each call pushes a frame onto the stack
Maximum stack depth equals maximum recursion depth
This is auxiliary space, not input space

practiceProblems.title: Finding Maximum
practiceProblems.explanation: We iterate through each of $n$ elements exactly once, performing constant work (one comparison and possibly one assignment) per element.

practiceProblems.title: Two-Pointer Technique
practiceProblems.explanation: Pointers start at opposite ends and move toward each other. Each iteration moves at least one pointer. Total iterations ≤ $n$, so $O(n)$ time with $O(1)$ space.
hints: Each iteration moves at least one pointer

practiceProblems.title: Building a Heap
practiceProblems.description: What is the time complexity of building a max-heap from an array of $n$ elements using the heapify approach?
practiceProblems.answer: $O(n)$ - not $O(n \log n)$ as one might expect
practiceProblems.explanation: While heapify takes $O(\log n)$ and we call it $n$ times, most nodes are at the bottom with small heights. The sum $\sum_{h=0}^{\log n} \frac{n}{2^{h+1}} \cdot O(h) = O(n)$.
hints: Most nodes are leaves with height 0
Only $\log n$ nodes have height $\log n$

practiceProblems.title: Constant Factors
practiceProblems.description: Why is $O(100n)$ simplified to $O(n)$ in Big O notation?
practiceProblems.answer: Big O describes growth rate, not absolute time
practiceProblems.explanation: As $n \to \infty$, the constant 100 becomes negligible. Formally, we can choose $c=100$ in the Big O definition. Both algorithms grow linearly—we care about the shape of the curve, not its steepness.
hints: Big O is about asymptotic behavior
Focus on what happens as $n$ gets very large

practiceProblems.title: Amortized Analysis - Dynamic Array
practiceProblems.description: A dynamic array doubles its capacity when full. What's the amortized cost per insertion?
practiceProblems.explanation: Most insertions are $O(1)$. Occasionally (when resizing), we pay $O(n)$ to copy elements. But resizing happens at powers of 2: positions 1, 2, 4, 8... The expensive copies are rare enough that average cost per insertion is constant.

practiceProblems.title: Quicksort Worst Case
practiceProblems.description: When does QuickSort perform at its worst $O(n^2)$, and why?
practiceProblems.answer: When the pivot is always the minimum or maximum element
practiceProblems.explanation: If we pick the first element as pivot and the array is already sorted, partitioning creates one subarray of size $n-1$ and one of size 0. Recurrence: $T(n) = T(n-1) + O(n) = O(n^2)$.
hints: Bad pivot selection leads to unbalanced partitions
One partition has $n-1$ elements, other has 0
This creates a linear recursion chain

practiceProblems.title: Hash Table Lookup
practiceProblems.description: What's the average and worst-case time complexity of hash table lookup?
practiceProblems.explanation: With a good hash function and load factor, elements distribute evenly—direct index access is $O(1)$. Worst case: all elements hash to same bucket, creating a linked list requiring $O(n)$ scan.
hints: Good hash = even distribution across buckets
Direct array access by hash index
Collisions can degrade to linked list traversal

practiceProblems.title: Master Theorem Application
practiceProblems.description: Use the Master Theorem to solve: $T(n) = 3T(n/2) + O(n^2)$
practiceProblems.explanation: Here $a=3$, $b=2$, so $n^{\log_b a} = n^{\log_2 3} \approx n^{1.585}$. Since $f(n) = n^2 = \Omega(n^{\log_2 3 + \epsilon})$ and $3(n/2)^2 \leq cn^2$ for $c < 1$, we're in Case 3: $T(n) = O(n^2)$.

practiceProblems.title: Nested Loop with Different Bounds
practiceProblems.explanation: Outer loop runs $n$ times. Inner loop runs $m$ times for each outer iteration. Total: $n \times m$. If $m = n$, this becomes $O(n^2)$.

practiceProblems.title: String Concatenation
practiceProblems.description:
In many languages, string concatenation in a loop is expensive. What's the complexity?
```python
result = ""
for s in strings:  # n strings, each of length k
    result += s
```
practiceProblems.answer: $O(n^2 \cdot k)$ or $O(L^2)$ where $L$ is total length
practiceProblems.explanation: Each concatenation creates a new string and copies all previous characters. First: copy $k$, second: copy $2k$, third: copy $3k$, ... Sum: $k + 2k + 3k + ... + nk = O(n^2 k)$. Use StringBuilder for $O(nk)$.
hints: Each `+=` creates new string + copies old content

practiceProblems.title: Tight vs Upper Bound
practiceProblems.description: Binary search is often stated as $O(\log n)$. Can we say it's $O(n)$? Is $O(n)$ a tight bound?
practiceProblems.answer: Yes it's $O(n)$, but $O(\log n)$ is the tight bound
practiceProblems.explanation: $O$ means 'at most.' Binary search is at most $O(n)$ (technically true but loose). The tight bound is $\Theta(\log n)$—it grows exactly as fast as $\log n$, no faster, no slower.
hints: $O$ is an upper bound, can be loose

practiceProblems.title: BFS Time Complexity
practiceProblems.description: What's the time complexity of BFS on a graph with $V$ vertices and $E$ edges?
practiceProblems.explanation: We visit each vertex once ($O(V)$) and examine each edge once ($O(E)$). In adjacency list representation, sum of all adjacency list lengths equals $2E$ (undirected) or $E$ (directed).
hints: Total work proportional to graph size

practiceProblems.title: Matrix Multiplication
practiceProblems.description: Standard matrix multiplication of two $n \times n$ matrices:
practiceProblems.explanation: Result has $n^2$ entries. Each entry requires $n$ multiplications and $n-1$ additions (total $O(n)$ work per entry). Total: $n^2 \times n = O(n^3)$.
hints: Result matrix has $n \times n = n^2$ entries
Each entry: dot product of two $n$-length vectors

def sort(arr):
    if len(arr) <= 1: return arr
    mid = len(arr) // 2
    left = sort(arr[:mid])
    right = sort(arr[mid:])
    return merge(left, right)
